title: My flesh is meat indeed (John 6:51–58)
hookLine: the Church reads this chapter as the heart of Eucharistic faith (CCC 1336)

lines: I AM YOUR BREAD: A METAPHOR?
cards: If a friend said, I am your bread, you'd take it as a metaphor. Up to now in John six, the crowd could too: bread from heaven, coming to him, believing in him, all of it sounds like a picture of faith.

Then Jesus says something no one can comfortably take as a picture, and the crowd starts arguing out loud. Christians still argue over this stretch of the chapter, and for Catholics it sits at the center of Sunday Mass.

teach.h: HOW CAN HE GIVE US HIS FLESH?
teach.b: Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "If any man eat of this bread, he shall live for ever; and the bread that I will give, is my flesh, for the life of the world."
The listeners argue: how can this man give us his flesh to eat?
He doesn't soften it: unless you eat the flesh of the Son of man and drink his blood, you shall not have life in you. And then: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed."
Meat is the old word for food; indeed means truly, really. Some readers notice that John's Greek changes verbs here, to one that can mean chew; others think it's only style.
The Church reads this chapter as the heart of its Eucharistic faith. The Catechism says this first announcement of the Eucharist divided the disciples, just as the cross would later scandalize them.

Catholics believe that at Mass the bread and wine become, truly and substantially, the body and blood of Christ, while still looking like bread and wine, and the Council of Trent called that change transubstantiation.
Orthodox Christians also hold that Christ is truly present. Protestant churches differ among themselves: some speak of Christ truly or spiritually present, some of a memorial.

Today's line, eat, and live, is the Catholic reading in three words: whoever eats this bread will live for ever. It's why Catholics genuflect to the tabernacle, and why the Church asks them to be at Mass every Sunday.
They believe they are being fed.

how: Catholics receive Communion at Mass believing it is truly the body and blood of Christ, genuflect toward the tabernacle where the consecrated Host is kept, and some spend quiet time in adoration before it.

games.q: what does “my flesh is meat indeed” mean?
o: a promise of quail in the desert again
his flesh is truly food, given for life
a rule about which meat may be eaten

p: the Council of Trent's word for the change
where the Host is kept, a lamp beside it

s: when the crowd objected, Jesus softened his words
he said it more strongly: my flesh is meat indeed, my blood is drink indeed.
Orthodox Christians also believe Christ is truly present in the Eucharist
Catholics and Orthodox both hold the real presence; Protestant churches differ among themselves.
the Catechism says this teaching divided the disciples
CCC 1336: the first announcement of the Eucharist divided them.

games.q: you've told a crowd your flesh is bread for the life of the world. they argue: how can he give us his flesh to eat? what do you do?
o: explain that it was only a figure of speech.
change the subject to the manna.
games.why: he goes further: unless you eat my flesh and drink my blood, you have no life in you. for my flesh is meat indeed.

practice: If a Catholic church nearby is open, you can sit near the tabernacle, where the consecrated Host is kept with a lamp burning near it; if not, picture one, the candle, the quiet, the box at the front.
Catholics believe Christ is present there, and some simply sit with him the way you'd sit with a friend, saying nothing. If you pray, just stay; if not, sit with the quiet and the lamp.

wordCard.voice: My flesh is meat indeed. Jesus in John six: his flesh is truly food and his blood truly drink. Catholics read it as the Eucharist. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: eating, chewing (John 6:54). John switches to this verb here; how much to make of that, readers debate.

carryVoice: Your line: eat, and live. That's week seventy-two: so loved, Saint Augustine, living water, white for harvest, made whole, bread of life, and meat indeed.
